passage: Ecological restoration has traditionally worked towards a picture. A degraded marsh or heath is compared with a reference state, usually the condition of the site at some earlier date as reconstructed from records, maps or surviving fragments, and success is measured by how closely the site comes to resemble it. Rewilding, in many of its versions, refuses this. Rather than aiming at a particular assemblage of species, it seeks to restore processes: grazing and browsing by large herbivores, the flooding of rivers that have been confined to channels, predation, the falling and rotting of trees. What the landscape then becomes is left open. Its advocates present this refusal to name an end state not as a gap in the method but as its central virtue.

Their reasons are serious. Any reference state is chosen, not found: a site has passed through many conditions, and to select one of them as the true or original form of the place is to privilege one moment of its history over all the others. Under a changing climate, moreover, the conditions that sustained a historical community may no longer exist, so that holding a landscape to an old picture would require ever more intervention, mowing, planting, culling and weeding on a scale that amounts to gardening, however large the garden. Better, the argument runs, to set processes going and accept whatever community they produce.

The obvious objection is that a project with no target cannot fail. If whatever emerges is by definition what nature has chosen, then no outcome, however disappointing, counts as evidence against the project, and those who fund it, live beside it or simply care about the place are left with no way to hold it to account. The objection becomes sharper when the results are unwelcome: when scrub swallows a flower-rich meadow that people valued, or when a rare species that depended on the old management quietly disappears. To answer that this, too, is nature taking its course is to make the project immune to criticism, and a claim that nothing could count against is not much of a claim.

Advocates have a partial reply. A project can be held to account for its processes even if not for its outcome: one can ask whether the river is in fact allowed to flood, whether herbivore numbers rise and fall with the food available rather than being fixed by managers, whether dead wood is left where it falls. These are checkable commitments, and a project that fails to keep them has failed in a sense that matters. But the reply does not dissolve the difficulty, because the choice of processes is itself a choice about outcomes. Which animals are released, in what numbers, within what fences and over how large an area will go a long way towards deciding whether the land becomes closed woodland, open pasture or something between, and often these consequences can be foreseen. A few cattle and ponies at low density on a large area will produce a different landscape from many of them on a small one, and those who set the density know this.

What rewilding achieves, then, is not the withdrawal of human choice from the landscape but its relocation, from the end of the process to its beginning. This is not an argument against rewilding, which may well be the most sensible response available in a world where no historical picture can be held still. It is an argument against a certain way of describing it. The phrase 'letting nature decide' conceals decisions that people have already made, and the method is more honest, and more open to the scrutiny it needs, when its advocates own those decisions.

options.B: Since every reference state is chosen and climate change puts old states out of reach, conservation should restore natural processes and leave the outcome entirely to nature.
options.C: Because a rewilding project without a target can never be shown to have failed, restoration towards a recorded earlier state remains the more accountable method.
options.D: Holding rewilding projects to account for the processes they restore, rather than for their outcomes, fully answers the charge that the method cannot fail.

passage: It has become common to say that colonial censuses did not so much count the peoples of the empire as invent them. The enumerator arrived with a schedule of questions and a list of permitted answers, and the population that emerged from the tables, divided into neatly bounded communities of religion, caste, tribe and language, was in this view largely a creation of the administrative imagination. The argument has done valuable work. It has made historians suspicious of treating census categories as simple descriptions of a pre-existing social order, and it has drawn attention to the way in which knowledge and rule were bound together. Yet in its strongest form it claims too much, and in claiming too much it obscures what was genuinely new.

The distinctions that census officials recorded were not conjured out of nothing. People in the societies being counted had long spoken of lineage, occupation, locality, sect and status, and had used these terms to arrange marriages, settle disputes and decide whom to eat with. What these older vocabularies did not usually require was that a person belong to exactly one category of each kind, at all times and for all purposes. A weaver might describe himself by his craft in the market, by his lineage at a wedding and by his village when travelling, without feeling that any one of these was his real identity. The census demanded a single answer, written once and then aggregated, and it treated a blank or a double answer as an error to be corrected.

The novelty, then, lay less in the categories than in what was done with them. Once fixed and counted, a category could be ranked, compared across districts, and used as the basis for decisions about recruitment, land and, later, political representation. Groups discovered that their recorded size and standing had consequences, and petitions asking to be listed under a different name or placed higher in an official order of precedence became a regular feature of census years. Some observers have treated such petitions as proof that the categories were artificial, mere labels that people manipulated for advantage. But the petitions suggest the opposite conclusion. People do not campaign over labels that mean nothing to them; they campaign over labels that have begun to govern their lives.

This is why the categories outlived the governments that produced them. An identity that is only imposed can be thrown off when its author departs. An identity that has been taken up, argued over and attached to rights and resources becomes part of the social world it was once supposed merely to describe. The census, in short, was neither a mirror nor a fiction. It was closer to a mould, into which existing and quite fluid materials were pressed until they set.

options.B: an instrument that gave a fixed shape to social distinctions which already existed but had been fluid.
options.C: a slow source of decay that gradually weakened the older identities until they disappeared from social life.
options.D: a faithful copy that reproduced the existing social order exactly as it was, without altering it in any way.

passage: Few medical ideas seem as self-evidently right as early detection. A disease found sooner is a disease treated sooner, and a disease treated sooner, surely, is more often cured. Screening programmes, which look for disease in people who feel perfectly well, are built on this reasoning, and the figures they produce appear to confirm it. People whose cancers are found by screening typically survive far longer after diagnosis than people whose cancers are found because they caused symptoms. Patients who have been through screening often say as much, and public campaigns repeat the message with understandable conviction. It is hard to imagine clearer evidence that looking early pays.

The trouble is that the comparison is rigged, though by the arithmetic of detection rather than by anyone's intent. Suppose a tumour will kill a woman at seventy whatever is done. If it causes symptoms at sixty-eight, she survives two years after diagnosis; if a scan finds it at sixty-three, she survives seven. Nothing about her death has changed, but the survival figure has more than tripled, simply because the clock was started earlier. A second distortion arises from the different speeds at which tumours grow. A test repeated every few years is far more likely to catch a slow tumour, which lingers in a detectable but harmless state for a long time, than a fast one, which may appear and cause symptoms between two tests. Screened groups are therefore loaded with the gentler cases, and their better survival partly reflects what was found rather than what was done.

The most uncomfortable distortion takes this tendency to its limit. Some of the abnormalities found by screening, though they look like cancer under the microscope, would never have grown enough to cause harm in the person's lifetime. Detecting them is called overdiagnosis, and it is not an error in the usual sense, since the cells are what the pathologist says they are. The error lies in the prediction that they would have mattered, and since such a lesion is removed or destroyed once it is found, the prediction is never put to the test. People with such findings are treated, sometimes with surgery or radiation, and they then appear in the statistics as survivors, which of course they are, though they were never in danger. Because no individual can know that his or her own tumour was of this harmless kind, every overdiagnosed patient experiences the treatment as a rescue. Screening thus produces its own most sincere advocates, and the more it overdiagnoses, the more grateful survivors it creates.

None of this shows that screening is useless. For some cancers, carefully conducted trials comparing large screened and unscreened populations have found fewer deaths among those screened, and those programmes deserve their place. The point concerns the evidence, not the verdict. The question to ask of a screening programme is not how long its patients live after diagnosis but whether fewer people in the population it serves die of the disease, and whether that benefit outweighs the harm of treating people who were never going to be ill. Survival after diagnosis cannot answer that question, because it improves under the influence of lead time, slow tumours and overdiagnosis even when not a single death has been prevented. Doctors are not immune to the appeal of the survival figure, since it describes the patients they actually see; the deaths a programme fails to prevent, and the needless treatments it imposes, are visible only in comparisons between whole populations that no single clinic can make.

options.C: fails her because the tumour is found too late in its course to be treated successfully.
options.D: lengthens the survival recorded after her diagnosis without postponing her death.

passage: There is a small puzzle about time that most people have noticed without ever stating it. A week spent travelling somewhere new seems to vanish while it is happening, so that there is never enough of it; yet once the traveller is home, the same week looks enormous, crowded with places and faces, as if it had lasted a month. A week at a familiar desk behaves in the opposite way. It drags while it is lived, each afternoon longer than the last, and then collapses in memory into a single grey item that seems to have taken no time at all.

The puzzle dissolves once we accept that we judge duration in two quite different ways. While an interval is passing, our sense of its length depends largely on how much attention we pay to time itself: boredom draws attention to the clock and stretches the hour, while absorption draws it away and the hour shrinks. Looking back, however, we have no clock to consult. We estimate how long a period lasted from what it left behind, and a period that left many distinct memories is judged to have been long. Novelty therefore works in opposite directions on the two judgements, shortening the interval as experienced and lengthening it as remembered.

This distinction sheds light on a complaint that becomes common in middle age, that the years go faster than they used to. The complaint is almost always retrospective. Few people find that a particular afternoon passes faster at fifty than at fifteen; what they find is that last year, viewed as a whole, seems to have been brief. If remembered duration tracks the number of distinct memories, the explanation is not far to seek, since adult life is more routine than youth, with fewer firsts, and a year of repeated weeks leaves less behind to measure it by.

The account is persuasive, but it should be held loosely. It is unlikely that a single factor explains how time seems at every age, and other changes, in health, in responsibility, in how far ahead people habitually plan, probably play a part. Still less does it follow, as some cheerful advice suggests, that one can lengthen a life simply by filling it with novelty. A crowded year may indeed look longer in retrospect, but it will feel shorter while it is lived, and there is no obvious reason to prefer one of these measures over the other. What the distinction teaches is not a technique for buying time but a caution against speaking of how long something 'really' felt, as though there were only one answer.

options.B: how pleasant or unpleasant the person finds the activity that fills the interval.
options.C: how old the person is and how routine the rest of his life has become.
options.D: how much attention is being paid to the passing of time itself.

passage: Visitors to shrines that are frequented by people of more than one religion tend to come away with one of two stories. In the first, the shrine is evidence of a deep harmony beneath official differences: here, at the tomb of a holy figure or a spring credited with healing powers, ordinary believers ignore the boundaries their clergy insist on and share a common devotion. In the second, the arrangement is a fragile truce, a curiosity that survives only until politics catches up with it. Both stories are told about sites around the Mediterranean, in the Balkans and across South Asia, and both, I think, misdescribe what sharing usually involves.

Close observation of such places rarely finds a single, blended faith. More often it finds parallel use. One community lights lamps in the evening, another comes on a particular weekday; one group knows the saint by one name and story, another by a different name and a different story, and neither is much troubled by the discrepancy. Custodians, frequently from one community, accept offerings from all and refrain from asking visitors what they believe. The sharing is real, but it consists in a set of practical accommodations rather than in agreement, and it works partly because certain questions are never posed: above all, the question of whose shrine it really is.

This is why the harmony story, attractive as it is, puts the emphasis in the wrong place. The arrangement does not depend on people believing the same thing; it depends on their not being required to settle what they believe about this particular place. Nor does the truce story fare better. Many such sites have been shared for generations, through periods of considerable tension elsewhere, which is hard to square with the idea that their peace is merely a pause. What usually threatens them is not the slow pressure of difference but a sudden demand for definition, when some authority, a government department, a heritage body or a movement seeking to purify practice, insists that the site be registered, restored or claimed as belonging to one tradition alone.

It would be romantic to pretend that these places were free of friction. Custodians could favour their own community, quarrels over offerings were common, and the vagueness that allowed sharing also allowed one side to quietly enlarge its claim. Still, the lesson they offer is more interesting than either of the usual stories. Coexistence, they suggest, need not wait for agreement about ultimate questions. It can rest on a carefully maintained ambiguity, which is a social achievement in its own right and, like most achievements, easier to destroy than to build.

passage: When a global fast-food chain enters a new country, the first thing commentators examine is its menu. If the chain serves the same burger it serves at home, critics see cultural flattening, the erosion of local tastes by a single corporate palate. If it introduces a spiced vegetable patty or a rice dish for the local market, its defenders announce that globalisation, far from erasing difference, accommodates it. Both sides agree, without ever saying so, that the menu is where the question of cultural influence will be settled.

That assumption deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. A menu is the part of a chain that is easiest to change and, for that very reason, the part that tells us least. What the chain actually exports is a format: a way of organising food, labour and time. The counter at which one orders without a waiter, the fixed price displayed in advance, the promise that the meal will taste the same today as it did last month, the kitchen run like an assembly line by staff who can be trained in days: these travel intact, and they carry assumptions about efficiency and predictability that are far more foreign to many food cultures than any particular ingredient. A spiced patty served through such a system is a local flavour in a global grammar.

Yet it would be wrong to infer that the format simply imposes its meanings wherever it goes, for customers bring meanings of their own. In some places a visit to a chain restaurant has been, at least for a time, a special occasion rather than a convenience: a clean, cool and respectable room in which a family can celebrate a birthday, or two young people can meet without attracting comment. The format was designed for speed, but the customers linger. They take a system built to minimise the time spent at the table and turn it into a place for spending time.

The interesting story, then, has three layers rather than one. The format is global and changes slowly; the meanings attached to it are local and can diverge sharply from what its designers intended; the menu sits between them, adjusted constantly in response to both. To read cultural influence from the menu alone is like judging the spread of a language by the loanwords it has picked up, while ignoring both its grammar and the uses to which its new speakers put it.

passage: Business journalism has a favourite kind of hero: the chief executive who arrives at a struggling company, takes bold decisions and turns it around. Magazine profiles, admiring biographies and conference speeches all tell the story in the same way, with the leader at the centre and everything else as scenery. The habit is understandable, since a firm is an abstraction and it is far easier to praise or blame a person than a set of market conditions. But the habit also produces a systematic error about how much any one leader actually controls.

Consider what else moves a company's results. Demand for its products rises and falls with the economy and with the fortunes of its industry; the price of its raw materials is set in markets it cannot influence; many of the products it sells were conceived years earlier, under managers who have since left. A new chief executive who takes over at the bottom of a downturn will, in the ordinary course of things, preside over a recovery, and the recovery will be credited to him. His successor, arriving at the peak, will be blamed for the decline that follows. Neither may have done much to cause what happened while he was in charge.

Imagine two firms in the same industry, with similar products and similar costs. One appoints a celebrated leader just as the market begins to recover; the other keeps an unremarkable manager who has run it for years. Both firms prosper over the next three years, but only one of them is written about, and the story of its revival will attribute to leadership what was largely a rising market carrying both firms upward. Such comparisons are rarely made, because the second firm has no story to tell.

None of this means that leaders are irrelevant. In moments of genuine crisis, or when a firm must choose between strategies that will shape it for decades, the judgement of the person at the top can matter a great deal. The error lies in degree, not in kind. Yet the error has consequences, for boards that believe in saviours go looking for them outside the firm, pay them accordingly, and dismiss them when results return to the ordinary, only to begin the search again. An organisation that understood how much of its fate lay beyond any individual might spend less on heroes and more on the people and systems that carry it through every leader's tenure.

options.B: explaining why business journalists prefer stories about individual leaders to accounts of markets and industries.
options.C: recommending that company boards stop appointing outsiders as chief executives and promote only from within.
options.D: showing that the effect of chief executives on results is commonly overstated, and that the overstatement is costly.

passage: The picture of the author that most readers carry is a picture of solitude: one person, one desk, one manuscript that emerges complete and is then merely printed. Publishing reinforces the picture at every step. The author's name alone goes on the cover, the author gives the interviews and accepts the prizes, and the acknowledgements page, where the other contributors are thanked, is the page readers most reliably skip. Yet anyone who has watched a book being made knows that the finished text is rarely the text the author first submitted.

Between those two texts stands, among others, the editor. At the broadest level, an editor may tell an author that the book begins in the wrong place, that a character is doing no work, or that the argument of a long middle section has already been made in its first ten pages. At the finest level, an editor queries a word, a comma, the order of two clauses. Much of this advice is accepted, some of it is fought over and some is refused; but the book that reaches the reader has been shaped by all three outcomes, since even a rejected suggestion can force an author to articulate why a passage must stay. The work is deliberately invisible. A good edit, like good stage lighting, is meant to pass unnoticed, and editors who want their contribution celebrated are generally thought to have misunderstood the job.

One tempting response is to declare that editors are secret co-authors and that the solitary author is a fraud. This overcorrects. In most cases the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention, and the editor works on what the author has made rather than making it; the relation resembles that between a performer and an exacting coach more than that between two composers. There are exceptions, cases in which an editor's cuts and rewritings have been so extensive that the question of whose book it is becomes genuinely difficult to answer, but they are exceptions precisely because they unsettle us.

The real lesson concerns how we assign credit rather than who deserves the most of it. Our habits treat authorship as an all-or-nothing property, possessed entirely by one person, when the making of most books is a graded collaboration in which contributions differ in kind as well as in size. Recognising this would not diminish authors. It would make it easier to see what they actually do, which is not to produce text from nothing but to direct a process that others help to carry out, and to bear responsibility for the result.

passage: Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub at a modest price and a large tub at nearly twice that. Most customers buy the small one, until the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub priced only slightly below the large. Hardly anyone buys the medium, yet sales of the large tub rise sharply, so that the new option has done its work without ever being chosen. It exists to make the large tub look like a bargain, and in many such cases it succeeds; marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it produces turns up often enough, with magazine subscriptions, holiday packages and software plans as well as snacks, to deserve a more careful explanation than the claim that customers are easily fooled.

The standard account of choice in economics assumes that a person arrives at a shop with a ranking of the available goods already settled, and that the shop merely reveals it. On that account the decoy should be inert: if I prefer the small tub to the large one, the arrival of a medium tub that I do not want should leave my ranking of the other two untouched. What the decoy suggests instead is that many preferences are not retrieved but assembled on the spot, from the comparisons the menu makes easy. The medium tub is easy to compare with the large, being the same product at almost the same price with visibly less popcorn, whereas the comparison between the small and the large, which requires trading money against quantity, is considerably harder. Consequently, people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

It would be a mistake to conclude that preferences are endlessly pliable, for the effect is strongest when buyers are unsure what they want and have little experience of the product; a regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat is rarely moved. It also weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick, and resentment at being steered can push them the other way. These limits matter, because they show that the decoy exploits a gap in knowledge rather than a defect of reason: constructing a preference out of whatever comparisons are available is a perfectly sensible strategy for someone who lacks better information.

The more interesting lesson concerns the menu itself. We usually treat the set of options as neutral background and the decision as the thing to be explained, but the decoy shows that the background is part of the decision. Whoever arranges the options, whether a cinema, a software firm setting its subscription tiers or a restaurant pricing its wine list, is not merely displaying choices but helping to form them. This does not make every arrangement sinister, since some arrangement is unavoidable, but it does mean that the question of what people chose cannot be separated from the question of what they were shown.

passage: Modern moral intuition tends to reserve its highest praise for the gift that expects nothing in return. A present given with an eye to what will come back seems to us slightly tarnished, closer to a trade dressed up in ribbon than to generosity. Anthropologists who have studied exchange in a wide range of societies have long found this intuition puzzling, not because people elsewhere are more calculating, but because in most places the obligation to return is understood as part of what a gift is. To receive is to accept a tie; to fail to reciprocate is not merely rude but a refusal of the relationship the gift proposed.

Consider how carefully the timing and size of a return are managed in many communities. A neighbour who sends back a dish of sweets on the very evening she received one has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed. A return that matches the original exactly carries a similar message. What sustains the bond is a return that comes later and differs slightly in value, so that one party is always, for the moment, a little in the other's debt. On this view the imbalance is not a flaw to be corrected but the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running: an account that is never quite settled is an account that remains open.

Seen in this light, the free gift is less an ideal than an anomaly. A gift that truly demanded nothing would create no tie, and a society composed only of such gifts would be a collection of strangers who happened to hand each other things. It is telling that the gifts we most often describe as free, such as anonymous donations, are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship between giver and receiver from forming.

None of this means that the obligation to return is always benign. Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay, the gift becomes an instrument of domination: the receiver is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence. Patrons have long understood this, and so have recipients of charity, who sometimes refuse help precisely because they cannot answer it. The lesson, however, is not that we should aspire to gifts without strings. It is that the strings must be ones the receiver is able to hold. A generous act, properly understood, is calibrated to the other person's capacity to reply.

passage: The familiar explanation of teenage recklessness is ignorance: adolescents take risks because they do not understand the dangers, or because they believe, in some half-formed way, that harm happens only to other people. If that were the whole story, the remedy would be straightforward. Teach young people the facts about speeding, drugs and unprotected sex, and their behaviour should improve. Schools and governments have spent heavily on precisely this remedy, and its results have often been modest.

One reason is that the premise is weaker than it looks. When adolescents are asked, in a calm setting, to estimate the dangers of various activities, their answers are often not very different from those of adults, and by the middle teens many reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do. What distinguishes them is less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations. Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature; decisions taken in the company of friends, under excitement, look very different. In laboratory games that reward bold choices, adolescents have been found to take noticeably more chances when they know their friends are watching, while the presence of an audience makes much less difference to adults.

A plausible account of this pattern appeals to the uneven timing of development. The systems that make rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense appear to become more responsive around puberty, while the capacities for restraint and planning continue to mature into the early twenties. For several years, then, the accelerator is more sensitive than the brake, and the gap shows most clearly when peers raise the value of a daring act. It should be said that accounts of this kind are easily overstated. Brains do not determine behaviour on their own, adolescents differ widely, and plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care.

If the account is broadly right, it has an uncomfortable implication for policy: the most effective interventions may be those that change the situations adolescents find themselves in rather than the beliefs they carry into them. Rules that limit the number of young passengers a new driver may carry, or arrangements that make the safe choice the socially easy one, work with the grain of adolescent decision-making rather than against it. The account also suggests a more generous reading of adolescence itself. A heightened sensitivity to peers is not simply a defect awaiting repair; it is part of what drives young people to leave the family, form their own alliances and try what their elders would not. The same disposition that makes a reckless dare attractive makes new friendships and new ideas attractive too.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, social scientists took it nearly for granted that modernisation and religion were locked in a zero-sum relationship. As societies industrialised, urbanised and educated their populations, faith would retreat, first from public life and then from private conviction. When the last decades of the century brought vigorous religious movements on several continents, and when religion returned to the centre of political argument in places where it had supposedly been tamed, many concluded that the secularisation thesis had simply been refuted. Some of its former defenders said as much.

Both the confidence and the recantation, however, rested on treating as one hypothesis what was really a bundle of several. One strand concerns differentiation: the process by which law, medicine, education, science and the economy come to operate by their own criteria, no longer answerable to religious authority. A second concerns decline: a fall in belief, membership and practice among individuals. A third concerns privatisation: the withdrawal of religion from public argument into the domain of personal choice. These claims are logically independent. A society could see religious practice flourish while its hospitals, courts and universities remain entirely outside clerical control, and that combination is in fact common.

Once the strands are separated, the evidence looks different. The decline thesis has fared poorly as a universal law; patterns of belief vary too widely between societies at similar levels of wealth to support it. The privatisation thesis has fared worse still, since religious voices are plainly present in public debate. But differentiation has held up remarkably well, and the point most often missed is that the religious resurgence itself tends to presuppose it. Movements that seek public influence organise as voluntary associations, compete for members, lobby legislatures, commission surveys and appeal to rights. They act, that is, as one set of claimants among many within institutions they do not control, which is precisely the condition that differentiation describes.

It would be too quick to declare the older thesis vindicated by this route. A theory that predicted the fading of faith and got that prediction wrong in much of the world cannot be rescued by pointing to the part that survived, and some of its proponents did expect the strands to move together. The more modest conclusion is that the debate has been conducted at the wrong level of generality. To ask whether the world is becoming secular is to ask a question with no single answer; to ask which institutions have slipped free of religious authority, and on what terms religion now competes for influence within them, is to ask questions that the evidence can actually settle.

passage: One influential account of curiosity holds that it arises from a gap between what a person already knows and what that person would like to know. On this view curiosity is not a general appetite for novelty but a response to a specific, noticed absence: the missing end of a story, the answer to a riddle, the identity of the person who has just telephoned. The account has much to recommend it. It explains why we are rarely curious about subjects of which we know nothing, since we cannot notice a gap in a field we cannot see, and why a little knowledge is often more stimulating than none. It also explains why curiosity so frequently vanishes the moment the answer arrives, leaving behind a satisfaction that is oddly short-lived.

Yet the information gap account fits some cases far better than others. It is at its strongest when the gap is well defined, as in a puzzle with a single solution or a mystery with a culprit. It is weaker when applied to the kind of curiosity that drifts without a target, the impulse that leads someone to wander along the shelves of a library, to turn over stones on a beach or to follow a footnote simply to see where it leads. In these cases there is no specific question waiting to be answered. If anything, the person seeks out situations in which questions might arise, and the pleasure lies as much in the searching as in any particular discovery.

Defenders of the account sometimes reply that the wanderer is simply responding to many small gaps in quick succession. The reply preserves the theory, but at a cost. If any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap, the account no longer explains anything in particular; it becomes a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis. It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds of curiosity, one that seeks to close a specific gap and one that seeks to encounter the unfamiliar, and that the influential account is a good theory of the first.

The distinction matters for anyone who wishes to cultivate curiosity, and for teachers above all. A lesson built on the first kind poses a sharp question and withholds the answer just long enough to make it wanted. A lesson built on the second provides a rich environment and the time to wander in it, without specifying in advance what ought to be found. Both have their place, but a classroom organised entirely around the first may produce students who are excellent at finishing puzzles and rather less inclined to go looking for them.

passage: In most schools a test is understood as a thermometer. It is applied at the end of a period of learning to find out how much has been learned, and like a thermometer it is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged. The understanding is so familiar that it seldom occurs to anyone that it might be false. Yet one of the more robust findings in the psychology of memory is that the act of retrieving something from memory is not a neutral reading: it changes the memory, and generally strengthens it, so that material which has been recalled once is more likely to be recalled again than material which has merely been seen again.

The contrast is clearest when the two activities are set against each other. Suppose two groups of students study the same passage, after which one group rereads it while the other closes the book and writes down whatever it can remember. The design holds constant both the material and the time spent on it, so that the only difference between the groups is whether they looked at the passage again or tried to bring it back unaided. Tested a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better; tested a week later, the group that practised recall tends to remember considerably more. The advantage of retrieval, in other words, is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked for so long by teachers and students alike.

What is more striking is how little the students themselves sense any of this. Asked to predict their own performance, rereaders tend to be the more confident group. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, in which the sentences are familiar and slide past easily, and ease of processing is readily mistaken for mastery. Attempting recall produces the opposite feeling, since it is effortful, it exposes gaps and it is often unpleasant, which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it. Teachers are not immune to the same illusion, since a class that has just reread its notes looks, and feels, better prepared than one that has just struggled to recall them. The method that feels like learning and the method that produces it are, at least here, not the same, and the lesson generalises uncomfortably: a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved.

It would be easy to draw from all this a crude conclusion, that schools should simply test more, but the finding does not support it. What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination, and the apparatus can work against the effort. A high-stakes test that provokes anxiety, or that is followed by no feedback, may teach students little except to fear tests, and a wrong answer recalled confidently and never corrected may itself be strengthened. The useful practice is humbler than the word 'test' suggests: it consists of frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study. None of this requires abolishing examinations, which serve purposes of certification that have little to do with memory; it requires only that they not be mistaken for the whole of what testing can do. Understood in this way, the thermometer turns out to be one of the more effective means of raising the temperature it was meant only to record.

passage: Ask people what grief involves and many will describe a sequence: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, and at last acceptance. The sequence has become so familiar that it can seem like a discovery about human nature, as settled as the stages of a fever. It began, however, as a description of how some terminally ill patients responded to the news of their own approaching death, drawn from clinical conversations rather than from any systematic study of the bereaved. Its migration from the dying to the grieving, and from a set of observations to something closer to a timetable, happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it.

When grief has been studied directly, the tidy sequence has not fared well. Bereaved people commonly report several of the named feelings at once, or in no particular order, and many report some of them hardly at all. Perhaps the most striking finding is how many people cope with a loss far better than the model would lead one to expect, experiencing intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages. Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise; for a good number of people it seems simply to be the ordinary course that grief takes.

The harm of the model lies less in its inaccuracy than in what people do with it. A description of what some people feel becomes a standard of what everyone ought to feel, and departures from the standard begin to look like problems requiring attention. The widow who is not angry may be told that she has not yet faced her loss; the son who feels relief after a parent's long illness may wonder what is wrong with him. Friends, and even professionals, may wait for a stage that never arrives, or press a grieving person to move on to the next one as though grief were a course with a syllabus.

It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity. It arrived at a time when dying and grief were seldom spoken of openly, and it gave people words for feelings, anger above all, that they might otherwise have hidden or been ashamed of. That was a real service, and it should not be forgotten in the rush to correct the record. The task now is to keep what the model offered, the permission to feel a wide range of things, while dropping the suggestion that those feelings must arrive in a fixed order, or arrive at all.

passage: The usual history of artificial light is a history of liberation. For most of human existence the coming of darkness set a hard limit on what people could do: work stopped, travel became dangerous, and the town shrank to the circle of the hearth. Oil lamps, then gas, then electricity pushed that limit back, until the night became little more than a dimmer continuation of the day, available for labour, commerce and pleasure. The story is not false. But it treats the night as an absence, a gap waiting to be filled, and in doing so it forgets that the pre-industrial night was a time with its own rules, its own inhabitants and its own uses.

In many European towns before public lighting, the night was governed differently from the day. Gates were shut, curfew bells were rung, and anyone abroad after dark without a lantern and a good reason might be stopped and questioned by the watch. The respectable stayed indoors; the streets belonged to watchmen, to those whose trades required darkness, to lovers, thieves and the young. This was not freedom in any simple sense, for the dark was also where violence went unpunished. It was, however, a separate jurisdiction, a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly and in which much that could not be done openly was done.

The first systematic street lighting was installed less to lengthen the working day than to bring this jurisdiction under control. Its sponsors spoke of safety, and they meant it, but safety meant visibility, and visibility meant that the street at midnight could be watched and policed by the same standards as the street at noon. Accounts from several cities describe crowds breaking lamps in moments of unrest, and it is tempting to dismiss this as mere vandalism. It is more plausibly read as a recognition, however inarticulate, that the lamps were an extension of an authority that the crowd had reason to resist. The lamp, in this sense, was an instrument of the day carried into the night.

Yet to replace the story of liberation with a story of discipline would be to make the opposite mistake. Lighting did extend surveillance, but it also opened the night to people who had been effectively shut out of it. Respectable women, families, the elderly and the cautious could now walk to a theatre or a shop after dark, and whole new forms of sociability, from evening promenades to late markets, grew up in the lit streets. For many people the expansion of the policed night was, quite simply, an expansion of their world. The same lamp that exposed the thief to the watch made the street usable for the seamstress walking home.

What lighting did, then, was neither simply to free the night nor simply to conquer it, but to abolish it as a distinct social time. The day's rules, the day's people and the day's activities spread into hours that had once belonged to others. Those who had held the dark, the watchmen, the night trades and the young, lost not their lives but their hours, and the newcomers to the lit street rarely noticed what had been displaced. Whether we count this as a gain or a loss depends largely on whom we imagine walking the street, and it is precisely the habit of imagining only one kind of walker that has made the history of light so easy to tell and so hard to tell well.

passage: The phrase most people use for the overland trade between China and the Mediterranean is a nineteenth-century coinage, and it carries a picture with it: a single road, and on it long caravans of camels carrying silk from one end of Asia to the other. The picture is attractive and largely misleading, for very few goods, and fewer merchants, made the whole journey. What existed instead was a chain of overlapping regional circuits, each worked by traders who knew their own stretch of desert, mountain and oasis intimately and knew little of what lay beyond it.

In such a system a bale of silk might change hands many times between the place where it was woven and the place where it was worn. Each exchange added a margin, which is one reason why goods from the far end of the chain were so costly, and each was made between people who had reason to trust one another because they met repeatedly. The merchant in an oasis town did not need to know the distant market where the silk would end up; he needed to know the caravan leader who would buy it from him and the one who had sold it to him. Long-distance trade, on this view, was an accumulation of short-distance relationships.

This has consequences that the romantic image hides. First, the system was more resilient than a single road would have been: when war or banditry closed one segment, goods could often find a way round it through neighbouring circuits, and trade slowed rather than stopped. Second, knowledge travelled poorly along the chain even when goods travelled well, and buyers at one end often held fanciful beliefs about where their luxuries came from, because no one they dealt with had seen the source. Third, those who profited most were frequently neither the producers nor the final buyers but the middlemen at the junctions where circuits met, whose cities grew rich on the margin.

It would be wrong to conclude that no one crossed the whole distance. Pilgrims, envoys and a few adventurous traders made extraordinary journeys, and some left accounts that are still read. But these travellers are remembered precisely because they were exceptional, and their fame has shaped our picture of the ordinary trade far more than the ordinary trade itself, which left few memoirs. A history built on the exceptional journey will see a road; a history built on the routine exchange will see a web, and it is the web that explains how the trade actually worked.

passage: It has become a commonplace, in philosophy as much as in popular psychology, that a self is a kind of story. On this view a person is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences but the narrative she composes from them: the account of where she came from, what she has struggled against and where she is heading. The claim is usually advanced in two forms at once. The descriptive form says that human beings do in fact understand themselves through stories. The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken.

The descriptive claim is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful. Some people report that they do not experience their lives as a plot at all. They feel little connection with the person they were a decade ago, find the invitation to tell their life story faintly baffling, and live with their attention fixed on present tasks and relationships. Nor is there any obvious sense in which their lives go worse: they form attachments, deliberate carefully and take responsibility for their conduct, only without experiencing their existence as an unfolding plot. It would be rash to assume that such people are simply unreflective, or that they are concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge. Their testimony is at least as credible as that of people who say the opposite, and it suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one.

The normative claim is more troubling. Stories have shapes, and the pressure to give one's life a shape is a pressure to select. Episodes that fit the arc are remembered and retold; those that do not are discarded or reinterpreted. Autobiographical memory is already reconstructive, and a governing narrative supplies it with a principle of selection that is rarely examined. A person who has told herself for years that she is someone who overcomes adversity will find it difficult to see the occasions on which she gave up, and harder still to learn from them. The demand for coherence can thus become a demand for a flattering kind of forgetting. A novelist may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot; a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs.

None of this means that narrative has no place. Making a promise requires regarding one's future self as continuous with one's present intention, and recovering from bereavement or injury often involves finding a way to tell what happened so that it can be lived with. Understanding other people, too, frequently depends on grasping the story they take themselves to be in. These are genuine goods, and a person who could never assemble any part of her past into an account would be at a real disadvantage.

But the goods enumerated here are those of an instrument, not of an essence. We use stories to bind ourselves, to heal and to understand, and we can use them well or badly, often or seldom. To say that the self simply is its story makes the instrument indispensable, and it turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency. The more modest view leaves room both for lives that are lived largely in the present and for the episodes that refuse to fit, and it may well be the more truthful of the two.

passage: For more than a century, the kilogram was a thing. Every measurement of mass in the world, from a pharmacist's dose to a shipping manifest, was ultimately traceable to a single cylinder of platinum and iridium kept under glass near Paris, against which official copies were periodically compared. When the definition was changed in 2019, so that the kilogram is now fixed by assigning an exact value to a fundamental constant of nature, the change was widely reported as the end of arbitrariness: the unit no longer depended on a lump of metal that someone had happened to cast.

That description gets the gain slightly wrong. The new definition is no less conventional in one obvious respect: the value assigned to the constant was chosen precisely so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as instruments could tell. Nobody wanted bags of flour to change weight overnight. Had the cylinder been cast a little heavier, the constant would have been given a different number. What the redefinition removed was not human choice but dependence on a particular object, and with it a peculiar kind of blindness.

The blindness worked like this. When the official copies were compared with the cylinder over the decades, they were found to have drifted apart from it by small but measurable amounts. Either the copies had gained mass, or the cylinder had lost it, or both; but because the cylinder was the kilogram by definition, there was no way, even in principle, to say that it had changed. A standard that defines itself cannot be found wanting. Whatever happened to it, it remained, officially, exactly one kilogram, and the masses of everything else silently moved with it. The world's weights were, in effect, being checked against a ruler that nothing could ever check.

A unit tied to a constant does not have this problem. Any sufficiently equipped laboratory can realise the kilogram from the definition, without travelling to a vault, and if two realisations disagree, the disagreement is a fact about the apparatus rather than about the unit. It must be admitted that the apparatus in question is elaborate, and only a handful of institutions can build it; in practice, most of the world still calibrates against physical masses, now traced to these laboratories rather than to Paris. Dependence has not disappeared. But it has become dependence on a procedure that can be checked and repeated, rather than on an object whose changes no one could ever detect.

passage: Ask most people how to tell a language from a dialect and they will offer a test that sounds admirably objective: if two groups of speakers can understand each other, they speak dialects of one language; if they cannot, they speak different languages. The test has the appeal of turning a question that looks political into one that looks empirical. One need only sit speakers down together, the thought goes, and see whether conversation succeeds. The test promises, moreover, to spare the linguist from taking sides in quarrels that are seldom really about grammar.

Unfortunately the test does not deliver what it promises, and the reasons are instructive. Intelligibility is a matter of degree, not of yes or no; it varies with the topic, the speed of speech and the listener's experience; and it is frequently lopsided, so that speakers of one variety follow their neighbours more easily than their neighbours follow them. Worse, it is not transitive. Across many regions, a traveller passing from village to village finds that each community understands the next without difficulty, while communities at the two ends of the chain cannot understand each other at all. Where on such a chain does one language stop and the next begin? Intelligibility alone gives no answer, and the boundaries actually drawn on maps tend to coincide with something else entirely: the borders of states, the reach of a written standard, the language of schooling and broadcasting.

Everyday usage of the two words confirms this. The Scandinavian languages are counted as several, though their speakers can often converse, each using their own; the spoken varieties of Chinese are commonly called dialects, though many of them are no more mutually intelligible than languages that everyone agrees are distinct. In each case the label tracks not the distance between the varieties but the presence or absence of a shared written form, a shared state, a shared sense of belonging together. A dialect, in ordinary usage, is very often simply a variety that lacks the institutions which would have entitled it to be called a language.

It is tempting to conclude that the distinction is therefore empty, a piece of politics dressed up as science, and some writers have drawn exactly that conclusion. It does not follow. That a boundary is drawn by institutions rather than by sound systems does not make it unreal, any more than the border between two countries is unreal because no river marks it. Whether a variety has a standard spelling, a literature, a place in the classroom and a name its speakers use with pride makes a large difference to how it is learned, how it changes and whether it survives. A variety used in schools and courts acquires words for law and science; one confined to the kitchen and the field tends to borrow such words, or to give way to a variety that has them. Those are facts about the social life of a variety, not about its grammar, but they are facts.

The mistake, then, lies not in drawing the distinction but in where we locate it. The difference between a language and a dialect is not a property of the speech itself, waiting to be measured; it is a property of the arrangements a society has made around that speech. To see this is not to abandon the distinction. It is to understand that when a community campaigns to have its dialect recognised as a language, it is asking not for a correction of the linguistic facts but for a change in those arrangements, and that the request should be judged on those terms.
